text: The last two lessons made Silver correct and genuinely incremental, handling late data without any special-case logic anywhere in the pipeline. Now it's time to build something brand new on top of that trustworthy layer: the Regional Manager's category breakdown, the second real Gold table this project delivers, answering a question the existing table was never designed to answer.

The Beginner project's gold.daily_sales_summary answers how each store did overall, one row per store per day. But it genuinely can't answer a different question: which categories are actually driving that number? A store's total could stay perfectly flat while electronics are climbing and apparel is sliding underneath it, and the existing table simply can't show that, because it was never grouped by category in the first place. So this is a brand-new table, not a change to the old one: gold.category_breakdown, one row per store, per category, per day.

In PySpark, this looks like reading silver.sales_clean, grouping by store_id, category, and sale_date, summing total_amount into total_sales and quantity into total_quantity, and writing the result as a Delta table with mode overwrite, saved as gold.category_breakdown.

The same aggregation written in SQL: create or replace table gold.category_breakdown as a select statement with those same three group-by columns and the same two sums, pulled straight out of silver.sales_clean. Either version produces exactly the same result, just a different syntax for teams that prefer plain SQL over PySpark DataFrames.

Notice this table doesn't get its own MERGE INTO anywhere — it's written with a plain overwrite, fully recomputed from scratch on every single run. That's a deliberate choice, not an oversight, and it's only safe because of the redesign in the lessons before this one: Silver is now kept correct by that incremental MERGE, and it's comparatively small, just one clean row per transaction rather than raw duplicate-laden Bronze. Because of both of those things together, recomputing a group-by over all of Silver every run is cheap and simple — there's no real benefit to adding incremental merge logic at this particular layer.

That's the real tradeoff this entire project is teaching: push the hard incremental logic down to Bronze and Silver, where the data volume is genuinely large, and keep the Gold layer as simple, fully-recomputed aggregations sitting on top of a trustworthy Silver. Next lesson, you'll confirm the original daily summary table still works exactly the same way it always did.
